spark.title: SQL vs. NoSQL Selection Guide
spark.summary: Choose between relational SQL (ACID, structured schemas, flexible joins) and NoSQL families (Key-Value, Document, Wide-Column, Graph) based on access patterns and scale.
spark.keyTakeaway: Default to SQL (PostgreSQL/MySQL) for structured, relational, or transactional data; reach for NoSQL when you need massive write throughput, schema flexibility, or native horizontal partitioning.
spark.byteSummary:
Choose between relational SQL (ACID, structured schemas, flexible joins) and NoSQL families (Key-Value, Document, Wide-Column, Graph) based on access patterns and scale.

Picking NoSQL too early forces you to re-implement joins and transactions in application code; forcing petabyte-scale time-series or high-churn key-value state into a single-node RDBMS hits write ceilings.

Default to SQL (PostgreSQL/MySQL) for structured, relational, or transactional data; reach for NoSQL when you need massive write throughput, schema flexibility, or native horizontal partitioning.

concept.whyItMatters: Picking NoSQL too early forces you to re-implement joins and transactions in application code; forcing petabyte-scale time-series or high-churn key-value state into a single-node RDBMS hits write ceilings. Most production architectures use **polyglot persistence**: [SQL](/domains/sql) for core financial/relational truth and [NoSQL](/domains/nosql) for sessions, feeds, and telemetry.
whenToUse: SQL (PostgreSQL, MySQL): financial ledgers, inventory, user accounts, complex ad-hoc queries, and strict ACID invariants.
NoSQL: Key-Value (Redis/DynamoDB) for sessions/caches; Document (MongoDB) for evolving catalogs; Wide-Column (Cassandra) for time-series/writes; Graph (Neo4j) for multi-hop networks.
whenNotToUse: Choosing NoSQL solely because "it's web-scale" when your dataset fits comfortably on a single vertical/replicated RDBMS.
keyPoints: SQL models **entities and relationships** first (normalized tables + joins); NoSQL models **query access patterns** first (denormalized aggregates).
SQL guarantees ACID transactions (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability); many NoSQL stores default to BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventual consistency) with tunable quorums.
Scaling: SQL scales vertically first, then via read replicas, federation, and sharding; NoSQL partitions horizontally out of the box via consistent hashing.
Modern convergence: PostgreSQL supports `JSONB`, while DynamoDB/CockroachDB/Spanner support distributed ACID transactions.

sections.content:
## Architecture & Trade-Off Matrix

| Criterion | Relational (SQL) | Key-Value | Document | Wide-Column | Graph |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Data Model** | Tables & Foreign Keys | `key -> blob` | JSON / BSON docs | Partition + Clustering keys | Nodes & Edges |
| **Consistency** | Strong ACID | Tunable / Eventual | Tunable / Strong primary | Tunable Quorum | ACID |
| **Joins / Ad-Hoc** | Native & Rich | None | Limited `$lookup` | None (query-driven) | Native multi-hop |
| **Best Use Case** | Orders, Ledger, Auth | Cache, Sessions | Product Catalog, CMS | IoT, Logs, Messages | Fraud, Social Graph |

_recommendedProblem.title: Active-Active Multi-Master Split-Brain Recovery
_recommendedProblem.prompt: Redesign an active-active multi-master relational replication pipeline between us-east-1 and eu-west-1 (6,000 writes/sec, 85 ms WAN RTT, < 15 ms p99 local commit) so a 9-minute transatlantic partition and 180-250 ms NTP clock skew never cause silent Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrites.
